introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0730 English Language 1, June 2022, Advanced Level). Duration: one and a half hours. Answer ALL the 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D. Choose the one that best answers the question, find the number of the question on the Answer Sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you score zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Do all rough work in the booklet. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. The paper has three sections: A Reading comprehension (questions 1-16, 16 marks), B Grammar (questions 17-38, 22 marks) and C Vocabulary (questions 39-50, 12 marks).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D.
incertitudes: Scan sans couche texte : les 7 pages ont été lues en image. Le passage de la Section A est recopié intégralement ; les repères [L5], [L10]... marquent les numéros de ligne imprimés en marge (placés après le dernier mot de la ligne imprimée). Les renvois (L13), (L19) et (L34) des questions 5, 6 et 8 correspondent à des lignes sans numéro imprimé, comptées à partir du début du passage.

Le passage imprimé contient des fautes conservées telles quelles : « folks use to search », « physique piercing », « Adolescent, and young adult feel very strong », « not unlikely the fashion houses » (pour « not unlike »), « where it come from », « he was able to draw the attention » (virgule au lieu d'un point), « get a sway », « All of these are not left with their own effects on the society », « makeups ». Une apostrophe ouvrante est imprimée sans fermeture avant « Our hair is a major source of pride and beauty. ». La source imprimée sous le passage est lue « http/.artdaily.cc/news/10651 » (adresse telle qu'imprimée, probablement mal reproduite).
Question 5 : la citation de l'énoncé (« often take place ») diffère légèrement du passage (« often took place »). Transcrit tel qu'imprimé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : toutes les clés sont établies par la règle de langue et le passage. Questions converties en OUVERTES (clé discutable, deux options défendables ou énoncé qui ne permet pas d'établir la clé), la réponse visée restant dans le corrigé : voir la ligne « Converties » ci-dessous.

Clés conservées en QCM mais moins certaines (option concurrente entre parenthèses) : Q1 A (C common people) ; Q8 A (guillemets de distanciation, C) ; Q10 D (B pass across a message to the shop owner, le texte parle du gérant et non du propriétaire) ; Q12 D (A, B, C sont proches mais disent « montrer qu'elles sont riches ») ; Q16 B (C neutral) ; Q18 D (in which, le seul qui s'accorde avec « apartment ») ; Q24 C (la proposition « that is functional » est une proposition relative adjective : l'option « adjectival phrase » emploie phrase au sens large) ; Q33 B (A Sleeping et D Due to sleeping sont grammaticalement possibles, B retenu pour la séquence des actions) ; Q38 A (C couldn't) ; Q46 A (C vicious est aussi un contraire de benign) ; Q47 D (la seule option qui n'est pas un synonyme, A, B et C étant proches) ; Q49 A (C working under unfavourable conditions).
Question 50 : l'énoncé imprimé (« choose the odd set ») ne dit pas ce qui rend un ensemble étrange ; la clé retenue (B, « nail » n'est pas un outil) est la plus défendable mais reste incertaine.

Points : aucun point imprimé par question ; les titres de sections annoncent A 16 marks, B 22 marks, C 12 marks, soit 50 questions à poids égal comme l'indique la consigne. Aucun écart de total à signaler.
Paper 1 : toutes les questions sont obligatoires (« Answer ALL the 50 questions »), donc aucune règle de choix.
Aucune figure ni photographie dans ce sujet.

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 3, 4, 11, 14, 15, 20, 31, 34, 45, 50. Q3 (deeds/actions synonymes), Q4 (A, B et D non établis), Q11 (superficial/sceptical), Q14 (peer pressure cause ou conséquence), Q15 (aucune option établie par le passage), Q20 (will have lived/will have been living), Q31 (is/are, tiret unique), Q34 (participle/adjective), Q45 (honest/just), Q50 (règle de l'ensemble impair non dite).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A - READING COMPREHENSION (16 marks)**

*Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions below.* *(The numbers in brackets, such as **[L5]**, mark the line numbers printed in the margin of the original passage, placed after the last word of the printed line.)*

**Passage for questions 1 to 16**

Fashion is a word that all of us use in our daily life on a regular basis. There was a time when folks use to search for certain fashion only for particular events, but as we speak, the trends have changed into part of everyday life for teenagers. It reflects in all they do, particularly within the luggage they carry, the clothes they wear and their foot gear, bracelets, hair styles, tattoos, physique piercing, makeup and so on. Fashion is not just an ambitious projected image of a reinterpreted good old value which fulfils some fashion or agenda, but is rather an **[L5]** evocative and refreshing concept worthy enough to be portrayed for society’s appreciation that makes us even more instinctive.

Today, dedicated followers of fashion look to cities such as New York city, London, Paris and Milan for their inspiration and to buy the latest trends. The concept of fashion trends developed in Europe, but what about fashion in the rest of the world? Early western travellers going to the East noted that fashion and styles changed **[L10]** slowly in countries such as Persia, India, China and Japan. However, this was not always the case as there was also evidence uncovered during the dynasty of Ming China of rapidly changing fashions in Chinese clothing. History shows us that changes in costume often took place at times of economic or social change, which occurred in ancient Rome and the Medieval Arabian Peninsula. Then a long period without major changes would follow. Periods of rapid change and movement of people influenced the textiles and styles that people **[L15]** chose to wear. Nowadays, people are still extremely conscious about the way they dress for various occasions. Adolescent, and young adult feel very strong about the brands they wear, whether it is for college, partying or sportswear. Their parents also feel the same about their own designer labels.

When it comes to fashion, most of us believe that we are individualists who can simply make up our own mind with what we wear each day. Therefore, not many of us would admit to being slaves to fashion. However, we **[L20]** are not just talking of the expensive fashion houses in Paris and Milan, which very few of us can afford, or would wear. We are talking of fashions and trends on everyday clothes, accessories, etc. It is the regular ones that we always wear such as jeans and T-shirts, the ones we feel comfortable wearing because they are cheap and practical. However, isn’t it true that these tend to be the same as the one every other person wears? Doesn't that mean that we like to be trendy? Of course, the large department stores to some extent, dictate what we wear. **[L25]** Furthermore, they keep our interest, not unlikely the fashion houses of Europe with their seasonal collections, or by announcing a festive sale. It is true that they always offer a choice, but they carefully select the clothing, which is trending at that time. We must realize that this extends far beyond the clothes we wear. It includes accessories, makeups and hairstyles. So, it is easy for us to say that we don't follow the dictates of fashion, but isn’t it true to say that we are all conformist at heart? **[L30]**

Some researchers carry out a study on fashion. They claimed that people who do not follow “normal fashion” get more respect from the others who follow. Most people view social status and competence of people who do not conform to “normal” ways of dressing. They discovered that the more outlandishly people dress, the more respect they get. Others who had a “weirder” fashion are considered to be more unique. Rather than think badly of someone scruffily dressed, many people believe that dressing down is a sign of confidence. Jessy says high-profile **[L35]** entrepreneurs who dress down may influence our views about fashion. Jessy’s experience in a fashion boutique was that a well-dressed young man entered that big textile shop, he was able to draw the attention of the salesmen who thought him rich and likely to make heavy purchases. He was shown the superior varieties of suit lengths and sarees. But after casually examining them, he kept moving to the next section, where ready-made goods were being sold and further on to the hosiery section. By then, the salesmen had begun to doubt his **[L40]** intentions and drew the attention of the manager. The manager asked him what exactly he wanted and he replied that he wanted courteous treatment. He explained that he had come to the same shop in casual dress that morning and drawn little attention. His pride was hurt and he wanted to assert himself. He had come in good dress only to get a sway and a decent treatment, not for getting any textiles. He left without making any purchase. All of these are not left with their own effects on the society. **[L45]**

A typical example of fashion victim is seen at the Temple Hair in India where thousands of women queued up to have their head shaved with a dry razor blade, leaving them completely bald. Within weeks, the hair would have been lightened and bonded on the hair of the rich Western women who want to imitate the hair of the rich and the latest red-carpet fashion. Does anyone dare to ask where it come from, or how much women are being paid to donate their locks to fashion? The shocking truth is that not a penny is given to the women who sacrifice **[L50]** their hair. In fact, they are not even told that soon it is going to be sold for profit. All the money goes to the temple itself. The Hindu temple is the second richest religious site in the world after the Vatican City, boasting up to 20 million pilgrims a year. The popular site costs \$120 million a year to maintain. Money mainly comes from donations, but the most prevalent source of income, however, is from the sale of human hair. Every day, up to 4,000 women visit the temple to take part in this religious rite. Lakshmi Srinivasan, a beautiful 21-year-old **[L55]** girl, lives nearby. From the age of 11, she sorted hair to export to the US. Indian women rub oils into their hair to keep it soft and beautiful. Also, they grow it very long. ‘Our hair is a major source of pride and beauty. Lakshmi, coming from a poor family, needed to work to feed her parents, as well as to save for a dowry so she could marry. But she had to make far greater sacrifices for their prosperity. ‘When I was younger, I was made to have my own hair cut off at the temple,’ she remembers. ‘My parents believed that it would bring us some luck, **[L60]** so I could not say no.’ Many poor families go to the temple to pray for good crops; for poor farmers, the sacrifice of hair to Vishnu adds to their chances of having a good harvest. And in LA, where looks are everything, women will pay premium prices to get their hands on temple hair. LA’s hottest shopping street, Melrose Avenue, is teeming with skinny blondes in designer clothes. The idea of ‘temple hair’ with all its spiritual connotations, has a special appeal in the city where religious fads are considered part and parcel of **[L65]** celebrity.

Teenagers are extremely conscious about how they look and often obsess over details that adults disregard as important. They do not dress up in the same way that we do. Some teenagers’ self-consciousness generates a horror of drawing too much attention to themselves. As a result, they go for the “not looking-very-dressed-up” look. Others enjoy getting all the attention they get and will wear just about anything to get it. Teenagers are **[L70]** probably the most fashion-conscious humans on earth. To them, fashion is incredibly important because it’s a way of showing the world who they are or who they want to be. Different teenagers have different personalities and for this reason, there exist clothes in different styles, sizes, colours, and fabrics. As people grow up, they form their sense of self through the clothes that they wear. Teenagers use fashion as a route to express themselves as well as their affiliations, gain social status and bond with their peers. **[L75]**

The adolescence phase is marked by the search for a personal identity and what adolescents wear plays a huge role in forging that identity. Teenagers express themselves through clothes and hairstyles. What a teenager chooses to wear is a way of individuating themselves and demonstrating how they want the world to see them. For example, teenagers who prefer wearing gothic outfits tend to have some associated traits like getting tattoos, piercings and applying dark make up. Peer pressure largely affects teenagers’ daily choices on matters like **[L80]** alcohol and drug abuse, fashion and style. Research has shown that teenagers will dress a particular way to stave off mocking and humiliation from peers. They feel that if they dress in inappropriate clothes, they could end up losing their friends. You will notice that teenagers will go shopping together or ask for advice on how to dress up for an event, say a birthday party. A majority of teenagers are influenced by people around them because they feel that they somehow need to fit in. Duplicating the fashion around them gives them a sense of belonging **[L85]** in today’s world. Teenagers will dress alike or keep friendship and bolster their self-esteem by ‘mirroring’. Teenagers will idolize the celebrities that they love. They look up to them for some fashion inspiration. When the teenager sees their favourite celebrity dressed in something that they love, they will go and buy the exact same outfit just to look like them. They will then show off the clothes to their friends. To sum up, fashion is closely interlinked with the history of the world. **[L90]**

*(Culled from the internet; http/.artdaily.cc/news/10651)*

*Choose the best answer for each question from the alternatives, A, B, C, or D.*

1. The word “*folks*” as used in the passage refers to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: In the first paragraph the writer says that “there was a time when folks use to search for certain fashion only for particular events”. “Folks” is an informal word for people, and nothing in the sentence limits it to one group, one social class or one territory, so it means people in general. B, C and D add a restriction (a particular group, ordinary or low-status people, the inhabitants of one land) that the context does not support. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 2. According to the passage, “*fashion*” is referred to as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The first paragraph says that fashion “is not just an ambitious projected image of a reinterpreted good old value ... but is rather an evocative and refreshing concept”. Option A repeats the idea that the writer rejects (“not just”), which is the trap. Options C and D rearrange words from the sentence but do not say what the writer says fashion is. The definition the writer gives is B. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: just an ambitious projected image of old values
an evocative concept that is refreshing
an interpretation of values and concepts which are appreciated
the projection of values that are worth portraying.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 3. Fashion can be reflected through people’s \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) deeds   B) actions   C) appearances   D) dressing
questions.corrige_markdown:
The first paragraph says that fashion “reflects in all they do, particularly within the luggage they carry, the clothes they wear and their foot gear, bracelets, hair styles, tattoos, physique piercing, makeup”. The list goes beyond clothes (hair styles, tattoos, piercing, make-up, luggage), so the best general word is appearances. Deeds and actions are near synonyms of each other and both describe behaviour, so neither can be the single intended key, and dressing is narrower than the list in the passage. The question is therefore not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the most defensible answer is C, but A, B and D can each be argued.

**Intended answer: C (appearances).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 4. According to paragraph 2, which sentence is NOT true?

*Options as printed:* A) Fashion designers can be found almost everywhere in the world.   B) Fashion scenes change with every season in many countries.   C) Socio-economic factors also account for changes in fashion.   D) Following fashion trends have not always been easy.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Paragraph 2 (lines 8-18, beginning “Today, dedicated followers of fashion ...”) says that fashion changed slowly in Persia, India, China and Japan, that a long period without major changes followed each period of rapid change, and that changes in costume often took place in times of economic or social change. C is therefore true. B is the statement that the paragraph contradicts, because it describes slow change in many countries rather than change with every season. A and D are not stated in paragraph 2 either, so the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the most defensible answer is B.

**Intended answer: B (Fashion scenes change with every season in many countries).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 5. When the writer says “*History shows us that changes in costume often take place in times of economic and social changes*” (L13), he means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The sentence at line 13 says that changes in costume happen at the same time as economic or social change. A restates this as coincidence. B makes the economy the cause of fashion, which the sentence does not claim. D reverses the direction (fashion causes the changes). C mixes the idea with the closing sentence of the passage. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: changes in clothing coincide with economic and social movements
the economic effects of fashion and the history of the world move hand in glove
fashion brings about economic and social changes in the world

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 6. The word “*individualist*” in (L 19) most probably refers to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: At line 19 the writer says “we are individualists who can simply make up our own mind with what we wear each day”. An individualist decides for himself or herself and does as he or she wishes. Being lonely (A), ignoring others (B) or showing no respect (D) are not what “make up our own mind” means. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

choix.texte: a person who is considered lonely
a person who does not listen to others
someone who does as they wish
a person who acts without reverence of others

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 7. The word “*trendy*” as used in the passage is a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: In “Doesn't that mean that we like to be trendy?” (lines 24-25), “trendy” follows the verb “to be” and describes the subject “we”: it is an adjective used as a subject complement. It does not modify a verb (not an adverb) and does not name a thing (not a noun). **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - parts of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 8. When the writer puts “*weirder*” (L34) in quotation marks, the insinuation is that he \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: At line 34 the writer reports how others see unusual dress: “Others who had a ‘weirder’ fashion are considered to be more unique.” The quotation marks (scare quotes) show that the word belongs to other people and that the writer does not accept it as his own judgement; the same sentence immediately calls such people “more unique”, which rejects the label “weird”. He is therefore distancing himself from, that is refuting, the opinion. B and D say the opposite. C is wrong because the opinion expressed is not the writer's own. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 9. According to the passage, who might be responsible for changing our perceptions on fashion?
questions.corrige_markdown: Lines 35-36 say “Jessy says high-profile entrepreneurs who dress down may influence our views about fashion.” High-profile entrepreneurs are well-known business leaders. Researchers only report a study (lines 31-34), and friends and designers are not said to change our views in this way. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 10. The motive behind the young man being well-dressed was to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The young man had come to the same shop in casual dress that morning and “drawn little attention”. He returned “in good dress only to get a sway and a decent treatment, not for getting any textiles” (lines 42-44), and the text says that the good dress did “draw the attention of the salesmen”. His aim was to make the salesmen take notice of him and treat him with respect, that is to impress them. He met the manager only after the salesmen began to doubt him, so C was not his motive, and the passage names no shop owner (B). A is not suggested. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: pass across a message to the shop owner
meet the manager of the shop

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 11. The salesmen in the shop are described as people who are \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) superficial   B) sceptical   C) satirical   D) stoical
questions.corrige_markdown:
The salesmen paid attention to the young man only because he was well-dressed (“thought him rich and likely to make heavy purchases”) and lost interest when his behaviour did not match his clothes. They judged by outward appearance, which is what superficial means. “Sceptical” (B) fits only the moment when they “had begun to doubt his intentions” (lines 40-41), so it describes one reaction rather than the people; satirical (mocking) and stoical (calmly enduring) are not supported. The two readings A and B are both arguable, so the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the most defensible answer is A.

**Intended answer: A (superficial).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 12. One major reason why western women have hair extensions is to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Lines 46-49 say the hair is bonded onto “the hair of the rich Western women who want to imitate the hair of the rich and the latest red-carpet fashion”. The women want to copy, that is emulate, the rich and famous. Options A, B and C say that the women want to show that they themselves are rich, famous or of high class, which the passage does not say. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: portray that they are rich and famous

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 13. From the passage one can conclude that Lakshmi had her hair shaved off because she \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Lakshmi says (lines 59-61) “I was made to have my own hair cut off at the temple ... My parents believed that it would bring us some luck, so I could not say no.” The hair was shaved because the family believed it would bring luck. A is wrong because women are not paid for their hair (line 50). C is wrong because she was “made to” do it, not because she wanted to. D refers to the dowry, which she saved for by working, not by giving her hair. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: wanted to earn some money for her family
believed it would bring her family good fortune
wanted to make a greater sacrifice for their prosperity
needed money to give her future husband

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 14. All except ONE is a consequence of fashion.

*Options as printed:* A) Individualisation   B) Mockery and humiliation   C) Peer pressure   D) False identification
questions.corrige_markdown:
The last two paragraphs mention individuating oneself through clothes (A), mocking and humiliation from peers that teenagers try to avoid by dressing in the accepted way (B) and peer pressure on teenagers' choices (C). “False identification” is not mentioned in the passage at all, so it is the odd one out. However, peer pressure is also a cause of fashion choices rather than a consequence, so C can be argued as well, and the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the most defensible answer is D.

**Intended answer: D (False identification).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 15. The author is of the opinion that teenagers should \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) not listen to their parents   B) listen to their parents   C) exhibit a more brand-oriented decision   D) not let opportunities pass them by
questions.corrige_markdown:
The passage describes teenagers' behaviour (peer pressure, imitation of celebrities, attention to brands) but never states what the author thinks teenagers should do, and none of the four options appears in the text. The only point where parents are mentioned is line 18 (“Their parents also feel the same about their own designer labels”). No option can be established from the passage, so the question cannot be marked automatically.

**No answer can be established from the passage (no option is stated or implied by the author).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 16. The writer’s opinion about man on fashion is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The writer calls the Temple Hair trade “fashion victim” behaviour, speaks of “the shocking truth” that the women receive nothing, and asks whether “we are all conformist at heart”. These choices of words show disapproval of the way people are controlled by fashion, so his opinion is negative. The tone is critical rather than neutral, and it is serious rather than sarcastic (there is no ironic praise). **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B - GRAMMAR (22 marks)**

*Choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best completes each sentence below.*

17. The population \_\_\_\_\_\_ the police for being \_\_\_\_\_\_ in the fight against criminality.
questions.corrige_markdown: The pair of words must make sense together. People praise the police for being relentless (never giving up) in a fight, so “acclaimed ... relentless” works. “Criticized ... efficient” and “condemned ... successful” make no sense because nobody blames the police for efficiency or success. “Admired ... brutal” is illogical because brutality is not admired in a fight against crime. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 18. I’d like to have an apartment of my own \_\_\_\_\_\_ I can invite my friends around whenever I want.
questions.corrige_markdown: A relative clause needs the preposition that goes with the noun it describes: one can invite friends around in an apartment of one's own, so the relative pronoun is “in which” (an apartment in which I can invite my friends around, that is, where I can). “Into which”, “for which” and “to which” do not match the action. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 19. She went abroad with a view \_\_\_\_\_\_ a business partner.
questions.corrige_markdown: The fixed phrase “with a view to” is followed by a gerund, because “to” here is a preposition: “with a view to finding”. The infinitive forms in A, C and D are therefore wrong. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
20. By next year, Ngum \_\_\_\_\_\_ in Douala as an internally displaced person for six years.

*Options as printed:* A) would have been living   B) will be living   C) will have lived   D) will have been living
questions.corrige_markdown:
“By next year ... for six years” looks forward to a point in the future and measures how long a situation will have lasted, so the future perfect is needed. The future perfect continuous “will have been living” stresses the duration of the situation (six years of living there). “Would have been living” is a past conditional and “will be living” does not use the “by” time marker. “Will have lived” is also grammatically possible in the future perfect simple, so two options are defensible and the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the expected answer is D.

**Intended answer: D (will have been living).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: 21. Do you mind opening the door? (*He doesn’t intend to*) \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: “Do you mind ...?” asks whether the action would bother the person. A person who does not intend to open the door is saying that he does mind, so the short answer is “Yes, I do (mind)”. “No, I don’t (mind)” would mean that he agrees to open it. “Yes, I don’t” and “No, I do” mix a positive word with a negative verb or the reverse. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 22. \_\_\_\_\_\_ were classmates.
questions.corrige_markdown: The pronouns are the subject of “were”, so they take the subject case (she, I). Courtesy and standard usage put the other person first and “I” last: “She and I”. “I and she” breaks the courtesy order and “me” is the object form. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 23. Jane lost her wrist watch. She can’t find it.
questions.corrige_markdown: The antecedent is the noun that a pronoun stands for and that comes before it. “Jane” is mentioned first and “she” refers back to it, so “Jane” is the antecedent of “she”. B reverses the relation, C uses the wrong word (precedent) and D calls the pronoun an antecedent as well. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 24. “We need a computer that is functional”. “*That is functional*” is a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: “That is functional” is a relative clause that describes the noun “computer”, so it does the work of an adjective. None of the options says “adjectival clause”; the closest is “adjectival phrase”, since the group of words has an adjectival function. It is not adverbial because it does not modify a verb, not a noun phrase because it does not name something, and not a mere verb phrase because it has its own subject “that”. The printed option C uses the word phrase loosely. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - clauses and phrases

questions.enonce_markdown: 25. “Wait a minute.” This is an example of a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: “Wait a minute” gives an order or request and has no stated subject (“you” is understood), so it is an imperative sentence. A declarative sentence states a fact, an interrogative asks a question and an exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 26. Choose from the alternative A, B, C and D, the sentence that is correctly punctuated.
questions.corrige_markdown: In C the exclamation is closed inside its quotation marks, a new sentence begins with a capital letter (“He called out.”), and the second speech opens and closes with quotation marks and starts with a capital. A ends with a closing quotation mark that was never opened. B puts a lower-case “have” after an exclamation mark and breaks the speech in the wrong place. D leaves the first word “Hey” without quotation marks although it is spoken. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

choix.texte: “Hey,” he called out. Have you asked about the missing telephone?”
“Hey,” he called out! “have you asked about the missing telephone?”
“Hey!” He called out. “Have you asked about the missing telephone?”
Hey! He called out. “Have you asked about the missing telephone?”

questions.enonce_markdown: 27. The new mayor appeared for the event in \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: When several adjectives come before a noun, opinion and description adjectives come before colour, and the adjectives that are equal in rank (well-cut, good-looking) are separated by a comma, with no comma between the last adjective and the noun. B respects both rules. A puts a comma between “well-cut” and “blue”, C puts the colour before the opinion adjectives, and D puts the colour before “good looking”. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: a blue good looking well-cut suit
a well-cut, blue good looking suit

questions.enonce_markdown: 28. We found \_\_\_\_\_\_ in the supermarket.
questions.corrige_markdown: The usual order of adjectives is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. Here the order is size (small), shape (round), colour (red), material (clay): “small round red clay pots”. All the other options break this order. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 29. Those are not my crayons, they are \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: To show that the crayons belong to James, the possessive form of a singular name ending in -s takes an apostrophe and an s: James’s. “James’s’” has one apostrophe too many, “Jameses” is a plural and “James” does not show possession. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

questions.enonce_markdown: 30. Please, come along with an umbrella \_\_\_\_\_\_ it rains.
questions.corrige_markdown: “In case” introduces a precaution taken because something might happen: “come along with an umbrella in case it rains”. “If” would make the umbrella a condition and change the meaning. “Should” alone needs inversion (“should it rain”), and “should in case” is not a construction. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
31. The bitter sweet flavour of motherhood - its joys, its sacrifices, its discoveries and its challenges \_\_\_\_\_\_ worth experiencing.

*Options as printed:* A) are   B) is   C) were   D) being
questions.corrige_markdown:
The head of the subject is the singular noun “flavour”; the list after the dash only explains what the flavour consists of, so the verb agrees with “flavour” and is singular: “is”. “Were” is the wrong tense and “being” is not a finite verb. However, the single dash makes the plural list read as the subject, so “are” is also arguable and the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the expected answer is B.

**Intended answer: B (is).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: 32. “Atom, your constant reluctance to take to advice will certainly lead you into problems.” This statement can be considered as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The speaker predicts a bad result (“will certainly lead you into problems”) if Atom keeps refusing advice. A statement that announces a coming danger is a warning. A suggestion would propose an action, a request would ask for something, and no help is offered. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown: 33. \_\_\_\_\_\_ late, Paul missed his flight.
questions.corrige_markdown: The perfect participle “Having slept” shows that the sleeping came before the missed flight and gives its cause; the subject of the participle is Paul, the subject of the main clause, so there is no dangling participle. “Haven slept” is not a form of English. “Sleeping late” and “Due to sleeping late” are weaker because they do not show the sequence of the two actions. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
34. Each participating school at the FENNASCO games received a prize. “*Participating*” is \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) a gerund   B) an adjective   C) a participle   D) a particle
questions.corrige_markdown:
“Participating” is the present participle of “participate” used before a noun to describe it (the schools that take part). A gerund would act as a noun and a particle is a small word such as “up” or “off”. Because a participle used in front of a noun also works as an adjective, B can be argued, so the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically: the expected answer is C (a participle).

**Intended answer: C (a participle).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - parts of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: 35. I have **drunk** two bottles of beer and I am **drunk**. These underlined words are \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: In “I have drunk” the word is the past participle of the verb “drink” and forms the present perfect with “have”. In “I am drunk” it follows “am” and describes the subject’s state, so it is an adjective. The order is verb then adjective. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - parts of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: 36. By practising five hours a day and \_\_\_\_\_\_, Esong became an expert football player.
questions.corrige_markdown: Items joined by “and” must have the same grammatical form (parallel structure). “By practising” is a preposition followed by an -ing form, so the second item must be “by sacrificing many ordinary pleasures”. A, B and D are a clause, a noun phrase and a verb phrase, which break the parallelism. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: because he made up his mind to succeed
was convinced that he could do it

questions.enonce_markdown: 37. “*In the heat of the war, everything on the path of the escaping rebels was set ablaze by them*” will be \_\_\_\_\_\_ in the active voice.
questions.corrige_markdown: To change a passive sentence to the active voice, the agent (“by them”, that is the escaping rebels) becomes the subject and the tense stays the same: the passive “was set” is simple past, so the active is “set” (simple past of “set”). B does this. A has a misplaced comma and no clear subject-verb order, C is still passive, and D changes the tense to the past continuous. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: “Everything on their path, the escaping rebels set ablaze”
“The escaping rebels set everything ablaze on their path”
“Everything on their path was set ablaze by the rebels”
“The escaping rebels were setting ablaze everything on their path”

questions.enonce_markdown: 38. You \_\_\_\_\_\_ be the one saying such things. It \_\_\_\_\_\_ speak well of you.
questions.corrige_markdown: “You shouldn’t be the one saying such things” expresses criticism (it is not right for you), and “It doesn’t speak well of you” states a present fact that supports the criticism, so A is coherent. “Mayn’t” is not used in modern English. “Couldn’t” would say that it is impossible that you are the speaker, which does not fit the second sentence, and “wouldn’t ... won’t” shifts the sentences into a hypothetical and a future that the context does not call for. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION C - VOCABULARY (12 marks)**

*For questions 39-43, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best completes each question.*

39. Bevy is to ladies as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: A bevy is a group of ladies, so the pair is a collective noun and the members of the group. “Bench” is the collective noun for judges (or magistrates), which gives the same relation. “Love”, “life” and “stem” are not collective nouns. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 40. If it is refuge you seek, you will only be granted it by swearing \_\_\_\_\_\_ to us.
questions.corrige_markdown: The word meaning loyalty is spelt allegiance: double l, then -egiance. The other options misplace the double l or write -ience. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

questions.enonce_markdown: 41. When the boy was bullied by his classmates, the comments didn’t even \_\_\_\_\_\_ him.
questions.corrige_markdown: “To faze” means to disturb or worry someone, so the sentence says the comments did not even disturb him. “Phase” (a stage) sounds the same but has a different meaning, “fez” is a hat and “fey” is an adjective. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 42. The decision we have taken is \_\_\_\_\_\_ revocable.
questions.corrige_markdown: The opposite of “revocable” (able to be cancelled) is “irrevocable”. Before a word that begins with r the negative prefix is ir- (as in irregular, irresponsible). “Un-”, “non-” and “in-” are not used with this word. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 43. I had a strong \_\_\_\_\_\_ that a disaster would occur and it did.
questions.corrige_markdown: A premonition is a strong feeling that something bad is going to happen. A prediction is a statement made about the future, forethought is careful planning and foresight is the ability to see what will be needed. Only “premonition” fits “I had a strong ... that a disaster would occur”. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For questions 44 and 45, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that is similar in meaning to the underlined words.*

44. He learned how **to walk on eggshells** around her after she threatened to leave him.
questions.corrige_markdown: To walk on eggshells is an idiom for behaving very carefully so as not to upset someone. After she threatened to leave him he became careful around her. Being nice, kind or loving describes friendliness, not caution. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown:
45. The **fair and square** policy of the Manager has made him very popular among the employees of the company.

*Options as printed:* A) clever   B) honest   C) just   D) relevant
questions.corrige_markdown:
“Fair and square” describes behaviour that is honest and follows the rules, with no cheating, and so the closest meaning is honest. “Just” is also close (treating people fairly), so the question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically; “clever” and “relevant” do not fit. The expected answer is B.

**Intended answer: B (honest).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For questions 46 and 47, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that is opposite in meaning to the underlined word.*

46. The lusty young man poked his sides out of admiration for the queen and stared at her in a **benign** manner.
questions.corrige_markdown: “Benign” means kindly or harmless, so its opposite is malignant (harmful, full of ill will). “Admirable” and “loving” are not opposites of kind. “Vicious” also describes cruelty, but “malignant” is the regular antonym of “benign”. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown: 47. His **ingenuity** is what made him a very famous person.
questions.corrige_markdown: Ingenuity means cleverness and inventiveness. Originality, resourcefulness and imagination are close in meaning to it, so none of them can be its opposite. Absurdity (foolishness, lack of sense) is the only option that points the other way. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - synonyms and antonyms

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For questions 48 - 49, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best explains the underlined expression.*

48. After the principal had flogged her, the disgraced Jane, retired to her room **to lick her wounds**.
questions.corrige_markdown: To lick one's wounds is an idiom meaning to withdraw and recover after a defeat or humiliation. The closest option is A, which speaks of soothing the hurt. Pondering (B) and crying (C) are only part of what the idiom suggests, and laughing (D) is the opposite of the mood. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

choix.texte: to soothe the wound in disgrace.

questions.enonce_markdown: 49. Following the ultimatum, the labourers found themselves **walking the tight rope**.
questions.corrige_markdown: To walk a tightrope is to be in a risky position where one false step has serious consequences. An ultimatum is a final demand backed by a threat, so after it the labourers were working under threat. Old tools (B) and long hours (D) are not suggested. C (unfavourable conditions) is a looser reading, so the most defensible answer is A. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For question 50, choose the odd set from the alternatives A, B, C or D.*

50.

*Options as printed:* A) orange, avocado, grape, mango   B) hammer, anvil, nail, saw   C) crocodile, whale, hippopotamus, shark   D) van, cab, jeep, motorbike
questions.corrige_markdown:
The question asks for the odd set but does not say what makes a set odd. Sets A (fruits), C (animals that live in or near water) and D (road vehicles) each name items of one clear kind. In set B, hammer, anvil and saw are tools but a nail is not a tool (it is something a hammer drives in), so the grouping in B is the one that fails. The printed question does not state its rule, so it is not reliable enough to be marked automatically and the best-supported answer is B.

**Intended answer: B (hammer, anvil, nail, saw).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
